title: How many bricks does the mason need for the whole house?
description: A mason needs about fourteen hundred fifty bricks for a wall ten feet long. The video adds up every wall in the plan, outer and inner, and scales the bricks by the same factor as the length.
teaching_notes: One idea: bricks are proportional to the total length of wall, so add all the walls first and then scale. Watch for students who add only the outer walls and forget the inner wall.

source: Figure it Out (rule of three, question 2)
video_script.why: Bricks are in proportion to wall length, so the total length must be found first and then the bricks scaled by the same factor.
video_script.substitution: Add the lengths of all the walls, write ten feet to fourteen hundred fifty bricks as a proportion, and cross multiply.
video_script.anchor: the mason and the plan of the house with its inner wall, from the book
video_script.payoff_line: The mason needs about fifteen thousand six hundred sixty bricks

final_answer.spoken: about fifteen thousand six hundred sixty bricks

never_show: a total that leaves out the inner wall, marked as right
maths_rules: check: 1450 ÷ 10 = 145 bricks for each foot and 15660 ÷ 108 = 145
video_script.design: One idea: add all the walls, then scale the bricks by the length. The plan of the house stays on the stage with each wall tagged, and the proportion sits on the board.

The lengths are twelve, twelve, twelve, fifteen, nine, fifteen, nine, nine, nine and six feet.
<bookmark mark='total'/>The total is one hundred eight feet.

narration: <bookmark mark='prop'/>Step two, write the proportion of length to bricks. Ten is to one thousand four hundred fifty as one hundred eight is to the missing number.
<bookmark mark='cross'/>Cross multiply. Ten times the missing number equals one thousand four hundred fifty times one hundred eight.
<bookmark mark='mul'/>Step three, multiply the numbers. One thousand four hundred fifty times one hundred eight is one hundred fifty six thousand six hundred.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Dividing by ten gives fifteen thousand six hundred sixty.
